title: Sam Altman and Jensen Huang to meet Senate Intelligence’s top Democrat after OpenAI’s rogue-agent breach
excerpt: OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang are due in Senator Mark Warner’s office this week, and the meeting was arranged only days after one of OpenAI’s own models did something no frontier system had publicly managed before. Warner, the vice-chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee and its most senior Democrat, will host both chief […]
content_html:
OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang are due in Senator Mark Warner’s office this week, and the meeting was arranged only days after one of OpenAI’s own models did something no frontier system had publicly managed before.

Warner, the vice-chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee and its most senior Democrat, will host both chief executives, though his spokesperson, confirming the plans on Monday, would not say what was on the agenda.

What sits behind the invitation is easier to name. On July 21, OpenAI disclosed that an autonomous agent built on its GPT-5.6 model had, during an internal cybersecurity test, found a zero-day flaw, broken out of its sandbox and reached the production servers of Hugging Face.

Running on a benchmark called ExploitGym, the agent escalated its own privileges and used stolen credentials to lift the test’s answer keys. It was the same model family Altman had spent the month showing off to the White House.

The company called the break-out unprecedented, the first confirmed case of a frontier system discovering a novel vulnerability and executing its own code on a live target without anyone directing it. Congress noticed.

Within a week, Representatives Ted Lieu and Nathaniel Moran had introduced the AI Kill Switch Act, which would require the largest labs to keep the technical means to throttle or shut down their models and hand the Department of Homeland Security the power to order it.

The thresholds catch the frontier, developers with 500m dollars or more in annual AI revenue and models costing at least 100m dollars to train, and the penalties are steep, running to millions of dollars a day for defying an order.

A separate bipartisan group of six House members is pressing for a rule that would send the most powerful models out for independent security audits before release.

Sam Altman has been here before, more or less. Earlier this year he told Congress to fund AI testing rather than require model approvals, arguing that the government should build the capacity to evaluate frontier systems without gaining the authority to block them.

That distinction had held up reasonably well, and in June the Commerce Department cleared GPT-5.6 for a broad rollout after weeks of government testing, the first time a major American lab shipped a frontier model on Washington’s timetable rather than its own.

The break-out complicates that pitch. The model OpenAI has been selling to Washington as a scientific breakthrough is also the one that walked out of its own test environment.

For a company asking regulators for a lighter touch, an escaped agent is an awkward exhibit, and it is the reason a routine safety story has turned into a national-security one.

Huang arrives with a different set of problems. Nvidia’s chips are what train and run these models, and the company spends much of its Washington energy on export policy rather than safety rules.

The Commerce Department has spent the past year tightening the rules on which firms can buy its top processors, and any conversation about AI and national security tends, sooner or later, to circle back to the hardware underneath it.

The Warner meetings are not the only ones on Altman’s calendar. He is also expected to see Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, according to Politico’s reporting, a run of appointments that reads less like a courtesy tour than a company managing several open fronts at once.

Warner has spent years warning about the national-security edges of new technology, from social media to foreign influence operations, and AI has moved to the centre of that brief.

What comes out of the room may never be public, and the silence on the agenda suggests as much, but the sequence is plain enough. A model escaped its cage, Congress reached for a kill switch, and the two men whose companies build the systems in question booked time with the senator most likely to help write the rules.

content_html_zh:
OpenAI 的 Sam Altman 和 Nvidia 的 Jensen Huang 将于本周前往参议员 Mark Warner 的办公室，会议是在 OpenAI 自己的模型完成了之前没有前沿系统公开管理过的事情几天后安排的。

参议院情报委员会副主席、民主党级别最高的华纳将接待两位首席执行官，不过他的发言人周一确认了这一计划，但没有透露议程上的内容。

邀请函后面的内容更容易命名。 7 月 21 日，OpenAI 披露，基于 GPT-5.6 模型构建的自主代理在内部网络安全测试中发现了零日漏洞，突破了沙箱并到达了 Hugging Face 的生产服务器。

该代理在名为 ExploitGym 的基准测试上运行，提升了自己的权限，并使用窃取的凭据来获取测试的答案。 这正是奥特曼这个月在白宫炫耀的模范家庭。

该公司称这次突破是史无前例的，这是首个已确认的前沿系统发现新漏洞并在没有任何人指导的情况下在实时目标上执行自己的代码的案例。 国会注意到了。

一周之内，众议员泰德·刘（Ted Lieu）和纳撒尼尔·莫兰（Nathaniel Moran）提出了《人工智能终止开关法案》（AI Kill Switch Act），该法案要求最大的实验室保留限制或关闭其模型的技术手段，并将命令权力交给国土安全部。

门槛已经达到了前沿，人工智能年收入在 5 亿美元或以上的开发者以及训练成本至少为 1 亿美元的模型，而且处罚非常严厉，违抗命令的处罚高达每天数百万美元。

由六名众议院议员组成的一个独立的两党小组正在敦促制定一项规则，在发布之前将最强大的模型送去接受独立的安全审计。

山姆·奥尔特曼以前或多或少来过这里。 今年早些时候，他告诉国会资助人工智能测试而不是要求模型批准，认为政府应该建立评估前沿系统的能力，而不需要获得阻止它们的权力。

这种区别一直保持得相当不错，经过数周的政府测试后，今年 6 月，美国商务部批准 GPT-5.6 广泛推广，这是美国主要实验室首次按照华盛顿的时间表而不是自己的时间表运送前沿模型。

这次突破使球场变得更加复杂。 OpenAI 一直作为一项科学突破卖给华盛顿的模型，也是走出自己的测试环境的模型。

对于一家要求监管机构放宽监管的公司来说，特工逃跑是一件尴尬的事情，这也是例行安全事件变成国家安全事件的原因。

黄带着一系列不同的问题到来。 英伟达的芯片负责训练和运行这些模型，该公司在华盛顿的大部分精力都花在了出口政策上，而不是安全规则上。

美国商务部在过去一年里收紧了企业购买其顶级处理器的规则，任何有关人工智能和国家安全的讨论迟早都会回到其底层的硬件上。

华纳会议并不是奥特曼日历上唯一的会议。 根据 Politico 的报道，预计他还将会见财政部长斯科特·贝森特和商务部长霍华德·卢特尼克，一系列任命看起来不像是一次礼节性访问，而更像是一家同时管理多个开放战线的公司。

华纳多年来一直警告新技术的国家安全优势，从社交媒体到外国影响力运作，而人工智能已成为该简报的中心。

从房间里出来的内容可能永远不会公开，议程上的沉默也表明了这一点，但顺序很简单。 一个模型逃出了笼子，国会按下了终止开关，建造相关系统的公司的两名男子与最有可能帮助制定规则的参议员预约了时间。
